description_full: Village Super Market, Inc. engages in the operation of a chain of supermarkets in the United States. The company offers grocery, meat, produce, dairy, deli, seafood, prepared food, bakery, and frozen food products. It also provides non-food products, including health and beauty care, general merchandise, liquor, and pharmacy products. The company offers its products under the Wholesome Pantry, Bowl & Basket, Paperbird, and Fairway and Gourmet Garage brands. It operates its supermarkets under the ShopRite and Fairway banners, and specialty markets under the Gourmet Garage banner; and online stores through shoprite.com, fairwaymarket.com, and gourmetgarage.com websites, as well as ShopRite app, Fairway app, and Gourmet Garage app. Village Super Market, Inc. was founded in 1937 and is based in Springfield, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Village Super Market, Inc. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $610M market cap on $2.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 7% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $55M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 14% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 3% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.33x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+14.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 36% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.45, it is more defensive than the market.
About $2.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 26% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 25% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 33% below its DCF fair value of $61.93, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $50.04 to $79.35 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 11.6 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 8.1 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 11.1 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 30% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 8.4% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 6.8%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).
It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.07x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $76.7M (13% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years, 3.5% over 5 years and 3.9% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 5.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.9% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 2.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 6, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 13.5% on average.
own: Insiders own 14.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 71%.
It returns 3.5% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 2.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years.
people: With about 2,130 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 2.2x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 3.8% a year.
That works out to $26K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (1x revenue per employee).
